strengths: The paper addresses a significant limitation of unsupervised sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in mechanistic unlearning, namely 'feature splitting', by proposing a supervised learning approach (SAEMNESIA) to enforce one-to-one concept-neuron mappings.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation is conducted on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, demonstrating a substantial improvement in average score (91.51%) over the recent state-of-the-art mechanistic approach SAeUron (82.29%) and other fine-tuning baselines.
The method significantly improves inference-time efficiency, reducing the hyperparameter search space by 96.67% since only a single latent feature needs to be steered per concept.
The paper evaluates practical scenarios such as sequential unlearning, adversarial robustness, and nudity removal (I2P), showing excellent scalability and robustness characteristics.
weaknesses: The requirement of supervised training labels limits the flexibility of the approach compared to fully unsupervised SAEs. If a new, unannotated concept needs to be erased post-hoc, the SAE would need to be retrained or fine-tuned on newly collected, labeled data.

The performance on nudity unlearning (Table 9) shows that the single-latent steering (base SAEMNESIA) is less effective (47 detections) than the unsupervised baseline SAeUron (18 detections), requiring the manual selection and steering of two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) to achieve better suppression. This suggests that the supervised one-to-one assumption may struggle on highly imbalanced or complex open-domain concepts.

The Concept Assignment (CA) loss in Eq. (8) only penalizes the lack of activation when the concept is present ($c \in T^{(b)}$), but does not explicitly penalize false positive activations when the concept is absent, relying instead on L1 sparsity and the unsupervised reconstruction loss. It would be beneficial to clarify why a negative supervision term was not included.

strengths: Identifies and successfully addresses a key bottleneck in SAE-based concept unlearning: feature splitting, which traditionally requires expensive post-hoc search over multiple latent combinations.
Proposes a novel supervised SAE framework (SAEMNESIA) that enforces one-to-one concept-neuron mappings (feature centralization) using readily available labels derived from text prompts.
Significantly reduces inference-time hyperparameter search by 96.67% because concept erasure only requires steering a single, predetermined latent.

Demonstrates strong quantitative and qualitative performance, outperforming SAeUron and other baselines on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, sequential unlearning, adversarial robustness, and nudity removal.
weaknesses: Relies heavily on structured prompt-to-concept pairings during training, which may limit scalability when attempting to unlearn complex, abstract, or highly fine-grained concepts where explicit text-based supervision is harder to construct.

The one-to-one mapping assumption shows limitations on highly imbalanced training concepts (such as nudity unlearning in I2P), where the base single-latent model struggles and requires steering multiple latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) to perform well.

strengths: Promising integration of mechanistic interpretability and machine unlearning, demonstrating how Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can guide concept steering in diffusion models.
Significant potential benefit in reducing the inference-time hyperparameter search space by striving for a localized, one-to-one mapping between concepts and latent variables.
Comprehensive evaluation covering a range of aspects, including the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, sequential concept removal, adversarial attacks, and NSFW content suppression on I2P.
weaknesses: Critical quantitative contradictions between the main text and the appendix: In Table 1, SAEMNESIA is reported to achieve UA=94.65%, IRA=91.39%, CRA=88.48%, and Avg=91.51%. However, Section 6.7 states that OS-DC-CA-FT is the model reported as SAEMNESIA in the main text. Looking at Table 5, OS-DC-CA-FT actually has UA=91.75%, IRA=93.16%, CRA=88.60%. The average of these three values is 91.17%, yet Table 5 lists the average as 91.51%. These discrepancies between individual metrics across tables and mathematically incorrect averages severely undermine the reliability of the empirical claims.

Conceptual contradiction of using supervised SAEs: The primary appeal of SAEs lies in their unsupervised, open-vocabulary feature discovery. Enforcing explicit prompt-level supervised concept-latent assignments shifts the framework toward supervised learning. The authors do not adequately justify why a complex SAE training procedure is preferred over simpler supervised baseline techniques (e.g., linear probes, concept bottlenecks, or supervised projection layers) when labeled data is already fully available.

Closed-vocabulary limitation: Because the centralization loss requires explicit labeled data (e.g., structured prompt pairs matching objects and styles), the method is restricted to a predefined, closed vocabulary. Forgetting a new or unforeseen concept would require collecting a new labeled dataset and retuning/retraining the SAE, which negates the flexible, open-ended utility of traditional SAE-based unlearning.

Failure of the single-neuron intervention claim on safety-critical tasks: The core thesis of the paper is that concepts can be cleanly erased by steering a single latent. However, for nudity unlearning (Section 6.11 & Table 9), steering a single latent performs poorly (yielding 47 detections compared to SAeUron's 18). The authors must resort to a multi-latent steering strategy (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) to achieve good performance, which directly contradicts the 'one-to-one mapping' claim and highlights the limitations of the supervised centralization approach when dealing with complex, real-world visual concepts.

strengths: Enforcing a one-to-one mapping between concepts and latent neurons via supervised training is a highly logical and effective solution to the feature splitting issue in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs).

Significant empirical improvements over the state-of-the-art SAE-based baseline (SAeUron), showing a +9.22% average accuracy boost on UnlearnCanvas object unlearning, and SOTA average performance across style and object unlearning combined.
Greatly improves inference efficiency by reducing the hyperparameter search space by 96.67%, since only a single latent needs to be tuned instead of complex combinations of multiple latents.

Comprehensive evaluation that includes practical scenarios: sequential unlearning (showing excellent scalability), adversarial robustness (under both white-box and black-box attacks), and nudity suppression (on the I2P benchmark).
Excellent analytical experiments, such as validating feature centralization using K-NN classification and visualizing latent activations and score distributions.
weaknesses: Requires supervised concept labeling during training. Although the authors demonstrate some generalization to unseen concepts in the appendix (Table 17), the performance drop compared to supervised concepts highlights a closed-vocabulary bottleneck.

The main evaluation is focused on the older Stable Diffusion v1.5 model. While this is standard in concept unlearning research, validation on more recent Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models is limited to a brief preliminary experiment in the appendix.

Some within-group concept interference still exists (e.g., unlearning cats affects dogs), as shown in the class disentanglement heatmaps in the appendix, though the authors rightly identify this as an open challenge.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and practical limitation of unsupervised Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for concept unlearning: feature splitting, where concepts are distributed across multiple latents, making intervention complex and search-heavy.

By introducing supervised concept-latent assignment and a dedicated composite loss (Concept Assignment + Decorrelation), the method achieves 'feature centralization,' enabling highly effective unlearning by steering only a single latent per concept.

The proposed method drastically reduces the inference-time hyperparameter search space by 96.67% (from a 2D combinatorial search of latents and multipliers to a simple 1D search of multipliers for a single latent).

Comprehensive and solid experimental evaluation on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements in unlearning accuracy (+9.22% average score over SAeUron) and scalability in sequential unlearning.

Extensive robustness and safety tests, demonstrating superior resilience against both white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial attacks, as well as effective nudity removal on the I2P benchmark.
weaknesses: The requirement for supervision during SAE training/fine-tuning (by defining concept-latent mappings via prompt-derived labels) limits the method's flexibility compared to fully unsupervised SAEs, making it less adaptable to open-vocabulary or dynamic unlearning scenarios without retraining or post-hoc scoring.

The decorrelation loss is only applied across macro-groups (e.g., objects vs. styles) rather than within groups, which leads to noticeable concept interference between semantically similar concepts (e.g., unlearning 'Dogs' still significantly affects 'Cats' generation, as shown in the appendix).

The evaluation is primarily focused on older architectures (Stable Diffusion v1.4/v1.5). While there is a preliminary test on SDXL-Turbo, there is no evaluation on modern Diffusion Transformers (DiTs, such as FLUX or PixArt), which represent the current state-of-the-art.

strengths: The paper addresses a key limitation of unsupervised Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in mechanistic unlearning—feature splitting—by proposing a novel supervised training framework (SAEmnesia) that enforces a clean, one-to-one concept-neuron mapping.
Enforcing feature centralization significantly simplifies inference-time steering, reducing the hyperparameter search space by over 96% compared to unsupervised baselines like SAeUron.

The method demonstrates strong performance across multiple benchmarks, outperforming SAeUron on UnlearnCanvas (objects) by 9.22% on average and showing remarkable scalability in sequential unlearning tasks (92.4% accuracy vs 64.0% for 9-object removal).
The inclusion of a decorrelation constraint between macro-categories (objects vs. styles) is mathematically sound and helps prevent cross-category concept entanglement.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, comprehensive qualitative results, and a thorough appendix that covers diverse architectures (SDXL Turbo), standard deviations, and detailed ablation studies.
weaknesses: Closed-vocabulary dependency: Since the method relies on supervised loss during training, erasing a new concept that was not included during training requires either costly retraining of the SAE or falling back to a weaker score-based assignment (as noted in Section 5).

Within-group interference: The decorrelation loss is only applied across macro-groups (e.g., objects vs. styles) but not within groups due to scalability issues. This leaves semantically similar concepts (like Cats and Dogs) susceptible to remaining entangled.

The scalability of one-to-one mappings to massive vocabularies (e.g., thousands of concepts) is unexplored and may require excessively large SAE expansion factors, posing a potential capacity bottleneck.
